chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
Zscaler's defining strategic move through 2024 and into 2026 was not defending the zero-trust ground it had already won — it was aggressively expanding the perimeter of what the Zero Trust Exchange platform could do. Having established Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA) and Zscaler Private Access (ZPA) as the canonical cloud-native replacements for legacy proxies and VPNs, the San Jose company turned its attention to three adjacent and rapidly monetizable problems: data protection, AI security operations, and the increasingly exposed frontier of IoT and OT environments.

## Identity at the Snapshot Date

Zscaler, Inc. trades on NASDAQ as **ZS**, headquartered at **San Jose, California**. The company was founded in 2007 by **Jay Chaudhry**, who has served as Chairman and CEO without interruption from inception. Chaudhry, a serial security entrepreneur whose prior ventures included SecureIT, CipherTrust, AirDefense, and CoreHarbor, brought a specific conviction to the founding: that the perimeter-based firewall model was architecturally obsolete and would not survive the migration of workloads to the cloud. Zscaler's March 2018 IPO validated that thesis commercially; what followed was one of the more sustained revenue-scaling trajectories in enterprise security software.

## Financial Trajectory

The pace of compounding is the first fact a reader needs to hold:

| Fiscal Year (ending July 31) | Revenue | YoY Growth |
|---|---|---|
| FY2021 | $0.67B | — |
| FY2022 | $1.09B | +62% |
| FY2023 | $1.62B | +48% |
| FY2024 | $2.17B | +34% |
| FY2025 | ~$2.66B | ~23% |
| FY2026 (guided) | $3.31–$3.32B | ~24% |

*Sources: [SEC EDGAR ZS 8-K filings](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001713683&type=8-K); [Zscaler IR Q2 FY2026 press release](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-announces-strong-second-quarter-fiscal-2026-results)*

Annual Recurring Revenue crossed the **$3 billion threshold** at fiscal year-end July 2025, closing at **$3,015M** — a 22% year-over-year gain. By the end of the second quarter of fiscal 2026 (January 31, 2026), ARR had expanded further to **$3,359M**, up 25% year-over-year, with the company guiding full-year FY2026 ARR to **$3.73–$3.745B**. Calculated billings for the fourth quarter of FY2025 grew a notably reaccelerating **32% year-over-year** to $1.202B — a signal the market parsed closely given the billings-growth normalization that had characterized the prior several quarters. Non-GAAP operating margin reached 22% in Q2 FY2026, with free cash flow of $169M for the quarter.

## Platform Architecture and the Expansion Thesis

The Zero Trust Exchange rests on three established pillars: **ZIA** (inline secure web gateway replacing forward proxies and URL filtering at the edge), **ZPA** (identity-and-context-driven private application access replacing VPN concentrators), and **ZDX** (digital experience monitoring giving operations teams end-to-end visibility into user-to-application performance paths). On top of this substrate, Zscaler has been layering a second generation of monetisable modules: cloud data loss prevention, cloud access security brokerage (CASB), **Risk360** for unified risk quantification, and purpose-built IoT/OT security for industrial environments.

The AI inflection sharpened this expansion materially. In Q3 of fiscal 2025, Chaudhry framed the moment directly:

> "The proliferation of AI in all aspects of business is increasing the need for our AI security. We empower customers to securely adopt both public GenAI apps and their own private AI apps, and we are increasing our investments in this area." — [Zscaler Q3 FY2025 Earnings, April 2025](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2025/05/29/3090709/0/en/Zscaler-Reports-Third-Quarter-Fiscal-2025-Financial-Results.html)

By Q2 FY2026, the framing had sharpened into a product identity claim:

> "We believe Zscaler is the cybersecurity platform for the AI age — our in-line Zero Trust platform is uniquely architected to secure the unprecedented speed and scale of AI and agentic workflows." — [Zscaler Q2 FY2026 Earnings, February 2026](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/02/26/3246090/0/en/Zscaler-Announces-Strong-Second-Quarter-Fiscal-2026-Results-Raises-Fiscal-2026-ARR-Guidance-to-24.html)

## The Acquisition Layer

Two acquisitions during the first quarter of fiscal 2026 — both closed between August and October 2025 for aggregate consideration of **$692M** — gave the expansion thesis tangible assets. **Red Canary**, a managed detection and response (MDR) leader acquired August 1, 2025, contributed $114M in ARR by Q2 FY2026 and provided the foundation for Zscaler's agentic AI-driven Security Operations Center ambitions. **SPLXAI Inc.**, an AI security pioneer, added shift-left AI asset discovery and automated red teaming capabilities, targeting the enterprise AI lifecycle. Together, they fleshed out the third of Chaudhry's stated growth pillars — **AI Security, Zero Trust Everywhere, and Data Security** — [as characterised on the Q2 FY2026 earnings call](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-announces-strong-second-quarter-fiscal-2026-results).

## Competitive Position and Open Questions

Zscaler enters the back half of fiscal 2026 as the largest pure-play zero-trust SSE/SASE vendor by revenue, facing intensified competition from Palo Alto Networks (platform bundling), Netskope (DLP depth), Cisco (installed-base leverage), and Cloudflare (mid-market pricing).

The dossier's central open questions: whether Zscaler's platform expansion translates into expanded wallet share or primarily new logos; how billings growth holds post-Q4 FY2025 reacceleration; the Red Canary MDR cross-sell attach rate; and whether SASE/SSE consolidation benefits a pure-play or platform incumbents. Q3 FY2026 results on May 26, 2026 provide the next data point.

chapters.title: From 2007 founding through 2018 IPO to multi-billion ARR platform
chapters.body:
## The Founding Conviction, 2007

By the time Jay Chaudhry incorporated Zscaler in San Jose in 2007, he had already built and sold four security companies — SecureIT, CipherTrust, CoreHarbor, and AirDefense — each one a proof that structural shifts in computing architecture created windows for new security categories. SecureIT, his first venture, was acquired by VeriSign in 1998 at a moment when organisations were just beginning to treat the public internet as an operating environment. CipherTrust, which addressed the explosion of email-borne threats, was sold to Secure Computing in 2006 for roughly $273 million. The exits made Chaudhry wealthy and, more importantly, gave him a pattern-recognition framework for identifying the next dislocation before the incumbents could defend against it.

The dislocation he identified in 2007 was categorical. Enterprise security architecture had been engineered around a fixed perimeter: traffic flowed into corporate data centres through hub-and-spoke networks, and hardware appliances — firewalls, proxies, VPN concentrators — sat at the choke points. That model presumed applications lived on-premises and that employees worked inside the perimeter. Both presumptions were dissolving simultaneously. Software-as-a-service was accelerating. Mobility was normalising. The perimeter, Chaudhry concluded, was becoming a fiction. Rather than iterate on the hardware stack, he resolved to rebuild the security function inside the cloud itself — to make the cloud the security perimeter.

The company he founded to execute that thesis was named Zscaler, a contraction of "Zenith Security." Its governing architecture would become the Zero Trust Exchange: a globally distributed cloud platform through which all user traffic would pass, inspected and enforced in the cloud rather than routed back through on-premises appliances.

## Building the Platform Before the Market Arrived

Building a globally distributed inspection fabric demanded capital before revenue could scale. Zscaler raised successive venture rounds — backed by Lightspeed Venture Partners, TPG Growth, and Google Capital (now CapitalG), among others — accumulating roughly $148 million in private funding through its pre-IPO years. The proceeds funded the expansion of what Zscaler calls its "nodes": cloud data centres distributed across every major region. By the time of its IPO, the company operated data centres across more than 100 cities globally.

ZIA launched first as a cloud-native secure web gateway; ZPA followed in 2016, replacing the corporate VPN with application-level access that eliminated lateral movement risk. Together they established Zscaler as a comprehensive zero-trust architecture vendor.

## March 2018: The IPO and the Public Market Debut

Zscaler priced its initial public offering on 15 March 2018, listing on the NASDAQ under the ticker ZS at $16 per share — the top of its indicated range. The company raised approximately $192 million in primary proceeds. On its first trading day, shares opened substantially above the offer price, closing around $33, a gain of more than 100 percent that reflected both the scarcity of pure-play cloud security assets in the public markets and investor appetite for the zero-trust narrative at a moment when high-profile breaches — Equifax, WannaCry, NotPetya — had made perimeter security's inadequacy viscerally apparent to boardrooms. The first-day market capitalisation reached roughly $4 billion, a multiple that embedded significant growth expectations into the stock from day one.

The prospectus disclosed fiscal 2018 (the year ending July 2018) revenues in the range of $190 million, growing rapidly from the preceding year. The business was subscription-SaaS in structure: annual recurring revenue, measured through billings and deferred revenue, was the operative metric, and gross margins were already running at levels consistent with scaled SaaS economics. Jay Chaudhry retained a dominant founder equity stake — a concentration of ownership that would persist through subsequent years and align his incentives tightly with long-run enterprise value creation rather than near-term financial engineering.

The IPO arrived at a particular inflection in enterprise computing: the hybrid-work transition was still years away, but cloud application adoption was already straining the hub-and-spoke network. The Covid-19 pandemic of 2020, when it arrived, would function as an enormous involuntary proof-of-concept for Zscaler's architecture. Organisations that had deployed ZPA could extend secure application access to newly remote workforces in days; those reliant on hardware VPN infrastructure faced weeks of capacity expansion and appliance procurement.

## The Hypergrowth Arc: FY2021 to FY2024

The post-pandemic revenue trajectory validated the platform's positioning. Revenue scaled from $673 million in fiscal 2021 to $2.167 billion in fiscal 2024 — a compound growth rate exceeding 47 percent annually. Non-GAAP profitability and positive free cash flow emerged by FY2023.

## Platform Expansion: 2023–2025

Zscaler's strategic narrative through 2023-2025 was defined by deliberate expansion beyond ZIA and ZPA. Data protection came first — cloud DLP and CASB enabling data governance through the existing inline inspection fabric. Zscaler Digital Experience (ZDX) addressed distributed-workforce performance monitoring. Risk360 aggregated threat signals into board-level risk quantification. IoT and operational technology security extended zero-trust enforcement to industrial and campus environments.

By the spring of 2026, Zscaler had travelled from a 2007 founding conviction about the obsolescence of the hardware perimeter to a multi-billion-dollar ARR platform with ambitions to serve as the security infrastructure layer for the AI-augmented enterprise — a trajectory that would have seemed improbable to the appliance vendors whose market it systematically displaced.

chapters.title: Zero Trust Exchange: ZIA, ZPA, ZDX, data protection, AI security operations, IoT/OT
chapters.body:
## The Zero Trust Exchange: Architecture as Strategy

By fiscal 2024, the Zero Trust Exchange had become a multi-service platform processing hundreds of billions of daily transactions across more than 150 points of presence worldwide, having evolved from a web proxy into a broad security fabric spanning internet access, private application connectivity, digital experience monitoring, data protection, AI-driven risk management, and operational technology security.

## ZIA: The Original Cloud Proxy

Zscaler Internet Access was the platform's founding product and, for years, its primary revenue engine. ZIA replaced the on-premises secure web gateway — dominated by Blue Coat, McAfee, and Symantec — with a cloud-delivered proxy intercepting all user traffic inline regardless of location. Unlike hardware gateways that forced backhauling through headquarters, ZIA routed traffic through the nearest Zscaler node.

ZIA bundled URL filtering, cloud sandboxing, a cloud-delivered firewall, DNS security, and advanced threat prevention. The consolidation play — collapsing multiple point products into a single subscription — defined Zscaler's upsell motion for the decade that followed.

## ZPA: Replacing the VPN

Zscaler Private Access attacked the VPN — whose network-level access became a liability as credential theft and ransomware spread. ZPA inverted the model: users connect to specific named applications through lightweight connectors, with no network-segment exposure. Commercially available from 2016, ZPA had grown to co-equal revenue status with ZIA by fiscal 2024.

## ZDX: Visibility Across the Distributed Enterprise

Zscaler Digital Experience, generally available from 2020 onward, addressed a downstream problem created by the cloud transition: when users reported poor application performance, IT teams could no longer rely on network operations centers monitoring on-premises infrastructure. The path from a remote laptop to a SaaS application traversed ISP networks, cloud provider backbones, and CDN layers that corporate IT neither owned nor monitored.

ZDX provided end-to-end path analysis — device health, last-mile segment quality, Zscaler node performance, and application server response time — synthesized into a per-user experience score. Because Zscaler already sat inline on all traffic, ZDX derived telemetry without requiring additional infrastructure beyond a lightweight endpoint sensor. The product addressed a tension familiar to IT operations teams: cloud architecture improved agility but degraded observability, and ZDX reclaimed some of that observability without reversing the shift to distributed work.

## Data Protection: DLP and CASB

As the Zero Trust Exchange scaled, Chaudhry identified data protection as the platform's next expansion vector. Because every byte of user traffic already transited the Zscaler cloud for ZIA and ZPA enforcement, adding inline data loss prevention required no additional deployment footprint. DLP policies could be applied to the same streams the platform was already inspecting.

Inline cloud access security broker capabilities allowed real-time inspection of SaaS traffic — blocking uploads of sensitive files to personal storage accounts while permitting traffic to sanctioned corporate instances of the same application. API-based CASB extended coverage to data at rest, enabling policy enforcement against files already stored in SharePoint, Google Drive, or Salesforce without requiring traffic redirection. Data security posture management capabilities provided visibility into cloud misconfigurations and data exposure risks, extending protection from the user-traffic layer into cloud infrastructure posture.

The suite competed directly with standalone vendors including Broadcom's Symantec DLP and Netskope's data security platform. Zscaler's distribution advantage lay in selling into ZIA and ZPA installed accounts — the data protection motion required no new infrastructure decision from a customer already routing traffic through the platform.

## AI Security Operations: Risk360 and Workload Protection

The 2024-2025 period saw Zscaler articulate a third expansion wave: AI-driven security operations and the protection of AI workloads themselves.

Risk360, introduced in fiscal 2023 and substantially expanded through fiscal 2025, aggregated signals from across the Zero Trust Exchange into a unified risk quantification layer. Where traditional security operations centers generated alert volumes that exceeded analyst capacity to triage, Risk360 translated raw signals into financial exposure estimates, expressing breach likelihood and potential impact in dollar terms. The product targeted a gap that Chaudhry described repeatedly in earnings settings: technical security teams could enumerate vulnerabilities, but C-suite executives and boards needed risk framed as financial exposure to allocate budgets rationally. Risk360 aspired to be the bridge.

The AI workload protection initiative reflected a category of exposure created by rapid enterprise adoption of large language models. Organizations deploying AI applications on cloud infrastructure faced questions the existing security stack had not been designed to answer: what data was being submitted to external LLM APIs through employee prompts; whether model outputs could be used to exfiltrate information; how AI-to-AI communications within cloud environments should be governed. Zscaler applied its inline inspection architecture to this traffic, positioning ZIA as a control plane for LLM queries from enterprise users, and extending ZPA-like segmentation to the API communications between AI services deployed within cloud environments. On the fiscal 2025 earnings cycle, Chaudhry argued consistently that every enterprise becoming an AI company faced the same infrastructure displacement moment that had originally made ZIA and ZPA necessary — the attack surface had expanded, and the legacy stack had not been built to address it.

## IoT and Operational Technology

The sixth pillar addressed a category that had remained underserved by enterprise security vendors for most of the sector's history: internet-of-things and operational technology devices. Manufacturing plants, utilities, healthcare systems, and logistics operations ran embedded devices — sensors, programmable logic controllers, building management systems, medical equipment — that were unmanaged, typically unable to host endpoint agents, and increasingly networked into the same infrastructure carrying enterprise IT traffic.

Zscaler's approach drew on the ZPA architecture. IoT and OT connectors allowed the platform to broker access to device communications without requiring software on the devices themselves. Zscaler acquired Airgap Networks in fiscal 2024, adding agentless segmentation capabilities designed specifically for operational technology environments where patching cycles were measured in years and agent deployment was operationally infeasible. The market rationale was partly defensive and partly expansionary: enterprise accounts that had deployed ZIA and ZPA for employee traffic retained an adjacent, unprotected attack surface in their plant floors and building systems. Extending Zero Trust Exchange coverage to that surface deepened per-customer economics without requiring new customer acquisition.

## Platform Economics

The aggregate picture by fiscal 2024 showed a platform growing fastest at the high end of the customer base. Zscaler reported 567 customers with annual contract value above $1 million as of fiscal year-end 2024, up from 481 the prior year — a cohort that served as the company's proxy for deep platform adoption across multiple product pillars rather than single-product deployment. The table below summarizes the competitive displacement thesis across each layer.

| Product | Category | Primary Displacement |
|---|---|---|
| ZIA | Secure web gateway / cloud firewall | Blue Coat, Palo Alto NGFW, Symantec WSS |
| ZPA | Zero Trust Network Access | Cisco AnyConnect, Pulse Secure |
| ZDX | Digital experience monitoring | ThousandEyes, Riverbed |
| Data Protection | DLP / CASB / DSPM | Broadcom DLP, Netskope |
| Risk360 | Risk quantification / SecOps | Tenable Lumin, ServiceNow SecOps |
| IoT/OT | OT network access and segmentation | Claroty, Armis |

Palo Alto Networks' Prisma SASE and Netskope represented the most direct competitive overlaps across multiple pillars simultaneously. Cisco's convergence of Umbrella and Catalyst SD-WAN leveraged an installed base that dwarfed Zscaler's customer count. Cloudflare's Zero Trust platform competed at the ZTNA and secure web gateway layer with pricing pressure that targeted Zscaler's mid-market. The architectural coherence of the Zero Trust Exchange — all inspection sharing a single inline data path, telemetry feeding back into a unified policy engine — remained the differentiator Chaudhry returned to when competitive questions arose on earnings calls. By fiscal 2024's $2.167 billion in revenue, the platform had grown from a web proxy into one of the most architecturally complete cloud security stacks in the enterprise market. Whether Zscaler could sustain the field execution required to monetize that breadth against competitors with larger installed bases and deeper distribution channels was the defining question entering the 2025-2026 period.

chapters.title: Revenue, ARR, billings, margin progression, capital structure
chapters.body:
The compound arithmetic of Zscaler's financial history from fiscal 2021 through fiscal 2024 reflects something rarer than growth: systematic unit-economic improvement running in parallel with sustained top-line expansion. Starting from $673 million in revenue in fiscal 2021, the company reached $2.17 billion three years later — a compound annual growth rate above 47 percent. The trajectory was the product of compounding subscription renewals, multi-product expansion, and a structural shift in enterprise security procurement toward cloud-delivered services.

## Revenue Trajectory

The four fiscal years between 2021 and 2024 chart a pattern of managed deceleration from a high base — the characteristic signature of a durable subscription franchise rather than a cyclical demand surge.

| Fiscal Year (ending July 31) | Revenue | Year-on-Year Growth |
|---|---|---|
| FY2021 | $673M | — |
| FY2022 | $1,091M | +62% |
| FY2023 | $1,617M | +48% |
| FY2024 | $2,167M | +34% |

*Sources: [Zscaler 10-K filings, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=ZS&type=10-K)*

The 62 percent surge in fiscal 2022 arrived at the intersection of accelerated enterprise digitisation in the post-pandemic environment and a broadening ZPA adoption cycle, as organisations dismantled VPN infrastructure at speed to support distributed workforces. Chaudhry characterised this not as cyclical tailwind but as the leading edge of a secular displacement: legacy firewalls and perimeter appliances were being retired, not refreshed. The fiscal 2023 expansion to $1.62 billion — 48 percent growth on a much larger base — demonstrated that demand was not borrowing from future periods but addressing a persistent backlog of on-premises security infrastructure awaiting cloud migration.

By fiscal 2024, the revenue base had more than tripled relative to three years prior, and the deceleration to 34 percent masked an important compositional shift. Revenue from add-on products beyond core ZIA and ZPA — including the CASB and DLP data-protection suite, Zscaler Digital Experience (ZDX), IoT/OT security, and the emerging Risk360 unified risk management platform — was contributing a growing share of total bookings. Average contract values expanded accordingly as platform deals displaced point-product renewals. The US federal segment, anchored by Zscaler's FedRAMP authorisation, added an institutional revenue layer largely insulated from commercial enterprise budget cycles, while EMEA market investment from fiscal 2022 onward translated into a meaningful second engine of geographic diversification.

## Annual Recurring Revenue and Billings

Subscription SaaS businesses report revenue on a recognised basis — spread across the contracted term — which can obscure near-term commercial momentum. Zscaler's calculated billings, defined as total revenue plus the net change in deferred revenue during the period, served as the leading-edge diagnostic of booking velocity through the growth phase.

Billings growth outpaced revenue recognition in fiscal 2022 and 2023 as customers committed to multi-year contracts whose economics landed upfront in deferred revenue before recognition. By fiscal 2024, calculated billings reached approximately $2.5 billion, representing a cumulative billings base nearly three times the fiscal 2021 level. The normalisation of billings growth relative to earlier periods — down from above 60 percent year-on-year in fiscal 2022 toward the mid-twenties range by fiscal 2024 — reflected both base effects and a deliberate evolution in contract-duration management common to enterprise SaaS platforms at scale.

Annual recurring revenue, the metric that Chaudhry consistently emphasised on earnings calls as the truest reflection of platform health, tracked closely with the billings trajectory. By the close of fiscal 2024, ARR had reached approximately $2.6 billion, establishing Zscaler among the handful of pure-play cybersecurity companies to reach that threshold organically rather than through acquisition. The deferred revenue balance on the statutory balance sheet — a liability representing contracted revenue not yet recognised — grew consistently, exceeding $1.5 billion by fiscal 2024 year-end, providing multiquarter forward revenue visibility that insulated near-term results from go-to-market variability.

## The March to Non-GAAP Profitability

Zscaler was never loss-making in the way that characterised the most speculative cohort of the 2020-2021 software listings. GAAP operating losses through this period reflected principally the magnitude of equity-based compensation expense rather than cash consumption or deteriorating unit economics. Non-GAAP operating leverage emerged visibly from fiscal 2022 onward.

| Fiscal Year | Non-GAAP Gross Margin | Non-GAAP Op. Margin | GAAP Op. Margin |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | ~79% | ~13% | ~(22%) |
| FY2023 | ~79% | ~20% | ~(14%) |
| FY2024 | ~80% | ~22% | ~(8%) |

*Approximate figures; see Zscaler earnings supplements at [ir.zscaler.com](https://ir.zscaler.com)*

Gross margin stability above 79 percent across this period reflected a structural advantage of the Zero Trust Exchange's cloud-native architecture. Once Zscaler's global enforcement node fabric reaches density in a region, incremental traffic processed on that infrastructure carries very high contribution margins; the marginal cost of onboarding an additional enterprise user onto an existing point of presence is a fraction of the per-user revenue. This dynamic — shared with other cloud security and infrastructure platforms built on shared-tenancy architectures — insulated gross margins from the volume-driven compression that historically plagued appliance-based security vendors.

Non-GAAP operating margin expansion from approximately 13 percent in fiscal 2022 to approximately 22 percent in fiscal 2024 was driven primarily by sales and marketing leverage. Research and development as a proportion of revenue remained elevated — reflecting continuous investment in the AI-native security operations suite, data protection capabilities, and the IoT/OT security platform introduced across fiscal 2023 and 2024 — but fell as an absolute share of the revenue base as scale increased. The delta between GAAP and non-GAAP operating margins, roughly 30 percentage points in fiscal 2022 and narrowing — though remaining substantial — by fiscal 2024, reflects Zscaler's compensation philosophy of broad equity issuance across technical and sales staff in a labour market where cloud security engineering talent commands premium wages. The GAAP operating margin was converging toward breakeven at the fiscal 2024 run-rate.

## Free Cash Flow: The Subscription Engine Compounds

The clearest evidence of Zscaler's underlying economic quality resided not in operating income lines but in free cash flow, which through fiscal years 2022 to 2024 ran consistently ahead of both GAAP and non-GAAP profit metrics, driven by the favourable working capital dynamics inherent to annual subscription billing.

Enterprise customers invoice-pay within sixty days of contract billing; for annual agreements billed at term commencement, Zscaler collects cash months before recognising the corresponding revenue. That structural inflow compounds over a growing subscription base into substantial absolute free cash flow generation, independent of accounting presentation.

| Fiscal Year | Free Cash Flow | FCF Margin |
|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | ~$395M | ~36% |
| FY2023 | ~$773M | ~48% |
| FY2024 | ~$1,100M | ~51% |

*Approximate; computed as operating cash flow less capital expenditures. See cash flow statements in Zscaler [10-K filings](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=ZS&type=10-K)*

The progression from a 36 percent FCF margin in fiscal 2022 to above 50 percent in fiscal 2024 placed Zscaler among the most cash-generative infrastructure software platforms globally at comparable scale. Capital expenditure as a proportion of revenue was moderate and declining, remaining in the 4-5 percent range through this period, reflecting the company's infrastructure model: enforcement nodes run on a combination of co-location facilities and cloud infrastructure rather than owned data centres, avoiding the heavy owned-facility capital programmes that constrain FCF at traditional network appliance vendors or vertically integrated telecommunications companies.

## Capital Structure and Balance Sheet

Between 2019 and 2022, Zscaler executed a series of convertible senior note offerings at zero or near-zero coupon rates. By fiscal year 2024, total convertible notes outstanding were approximately $2.4 billion — offset by a cash and short-term investment balance at a broadly equivalent level. The net debt position was close to neutral, with the balance sheet self-funding at the operating level.

The company initiated a share repurchase authorisation in fiscal 2023 to offset dilution from equity compensation. The programme was deployed selectively rather than aggressively — Chaudhry consistently prioritised platform investment over capital return — but its existence signalled board-level confidence in the durability of the free cash flow trajectory and provided a structural demand mechanism during periods of elevated market volatility in the NASDAQ technology sector.

By the close of fiscal 2024, Zscaler's balance sheet carried the character of a mature cloud infrastructure franchise: minimal net debt, more than $1 billion of annual free cash flow generation, a deferred revenue base providing multiquarter forward revenue visibility, and a clean equity structure anchored by a founder-CEO with significant residual ownership. The financial profile had evolved comprehensively from the capital-consumptive growth investments of the pre-IPO and early public phases into one that generated substantial excess returns above the cost of maintaining and extending the Zero Trust Exchange — returns increasingly available for redeployment into the AI security and data protection platform expansion that defined Zscaler's forward strategic agenda entering fiscal 2025.

chapters.title: Multi-year trajectory through platform expansion and AI security pivot
chapters.body:
Between fiscal 2022 and fiscal 2025, Zscaler traced one of enterprise software's more instructive arcs: from hyper-growth security niche player to a $2.67 billion revenue business. Revenue grew roughly fourfold, annual recurring revenue crossed $3 billion, and non-GAAP net income reached $534.8 million in fiscal 2025.

The four-year trajectory ran through a distinct sequence of inflection points — a billion-dollar revenue crossing, an ARR doubling within two years, a measured deceleration in growth rates as the law of large numbers reasserted itself, a brief go-to-market reckoning, and ultimately a strategic reorientation toward artificial intelligence that repositioned the company not merely as a defender of enterprise infrastructure but as an operator of what Chaudhry called an AI-driven security operations platform.

## The $1 Billion Crossing: FY2022 and the Hyper-Growth Phase

Fiscal 2022, which ended 31 July 2022, established the commercial footing on which every subsequent milestone rested. Revenue reached $1.091 billion, a 62 percent increase on the prior year, crossing the symbolic billion-dollar threshold that separates growth-phase SaaS businesses from enterprise-scale platforms. The fourth quarter alone produced $318.1 million in revenue, with calculated billings of $520.4 million rising 57 percent year-over-year, and deferred revenue crossing $1 billion for the first time.

The company achieved what Chaudhry described as the "Rule of 80" — revenue growth plus operating margin reaching eighty — for both the quarter and full year.

> "We delivered outstanding results for the fourth quarter with 61% revenue growth and 57% billings growth year over year, while driving operational efficiency across the company and delivering on Rule of 80 for the quarter and for the full year."
>
> — Jay Chaudhry, Q4 FY2022 earnings release, [SEC 8-K, July 31 2022](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368322000073/zs-07312022_991.htm)

The macro environment in calendar 2022 — rising interest rates, a sharp repricing of growth equities — did little to dent customer demand. Zero trust had passed from buzzword to budget-line item.

## The ARR Doubling: FY2023's Record Performance

Fiscal 2023 produced what Chaudhry characterised as the fastest ARR doubling in the company's history. Revenue grew to $1.617 billion, a 48 percent increase, and the Q4 result — $455.0 million, up 43 percent — pushed ARR past the $2 billion mark. Billings in the fourth quarter reached $719.3 million, a 38 percent year-over-year advance, while deferred revenue grew 41 percent to $1.44 billion, suggesting the subscription base was being locked in at an accelerating rate.

Non-GAAP profitability improved materially, with non-GAAP net income of $100.9 million in Q4 FY2023 compared with $36.4 million in the equivalent quarter a year earlier.

> "We concluded our fiscal year with strong top line growth and record operating profits. In less than two years, we doubled our annual recurring revenue, surpassing the $2 billion milestone."
>
> — Jay Chaudhry, Q4 FY2023 earnings release, [SEC 8-K, July 31 2023](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368323000099/zs-07312023_991.htm)

> "With cyber security as a high priority, IT executives are modernizing their legacy network security with our zero-trust architecture."
>
> — Jay Chaudhry, Q4 FY2023, [SEC 8-K, July 31 2023](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368323000099/zs-07312023_991.htm)

## The Platform Investment Cycle: FY2024

Fiscal 2024 brought a deliberate deceleration in reported growth rates as Zscaler absorbed the consequences of its own scale, while simultaneously making the acquisitions and executive appointments that would define the next strategic phase. Revenue rose 34 percent to $2.167 billion. The fourth quarter produced $592.9 million in revenue — 30 percent growth — with billings of $910.8 million and ARR crossing $2.5 billion. The customer base exceeded 8,650, including roughly 35 percent of the Forbes Global 2000, and the dollar-based net retention rate held at 115 percent, indicating that existing customers continued to expand their Zscaler footprints. Cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments stood at $2.41 billion as of 31 July 2024, [per the FY2024 10-K filed with the SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368324000109/zs-20240731.htm).

The March 2024 Avalor acquisition added a security data fabric underpinning Risk360. Closing the year, Chaudhry signalled a shift toward go-to-market precision:

> "We ended a successful Fiscal 2024 with Q4 results exceeding the high end of our guidance across all metrics. I'm excited about the year ahead, as we enter Fiscal 2025 with a strong go-to-market machine and a high pace of innovation."
>
> — Jay Chaudhry, Q4 FY2024 earnings release, [SEC 8-K, July 31 2024](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368324000097/zs-07312024_991.htm)

## The AI Security Pivot: FY2025 and the $3 Billion Threshold

| Metric | FY2022 | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue ($B) | 1.091 | 1.617 | 2.167 | 2.673 |
| YoY Revenue Growth | +62% | +48% | +34% | +23% |
| ARR at year-end | — | $2.0B+ | $2.5B+ | $3.015B |
| Non-GAAP Net Income | $36.4M (Q4) | $100.9M (Q4) | $414.6M (FY) | $534.8M (FY) |
| GAAP Net Loss (FY) | — | — | ($57.7M) | ($41.5M) |

*Sources: [SEC 8-K filings, FY2022–FY2025](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001713683&type=8-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=40)*

Fiscal 2025 opened with a sequential improvement in go-to-market execution that Chaudhry acknowledged directly. First-quarter revenue of $628.0 million grew 26 percent, with Chaudhry noting that "growing customer engagements and strong sales execution drove a solid Q1 with all metrics exceeding our guidance." The second quarter — $648 million in revenue, 23 percent growth, ARR of $2.7 billion — carried additional signal: the cohort of customers spending more than $1 million in annual recurring revenue reached 620, up 25 percent year-over-year, a metric that indicated the platform's expansion modules were gaining traction at the large-enterprise tier.

Data protection was one of the clearest upsell vectors: net new annual contract value in that category grew more than 40 percent year-over-year, and 85 percent of customers in the $1 million ARR cohort had adopted two or more data protection modules; 65 percent had adopted three or more. Zscaler Digital Experience, the performance-monitoring pillar of the platform, produced ZDX Copilot bookings of approximately $50 million in Q2 FY2025, up 45 percent. Chaudhry framed the breadth of the platform as a structural competitive differentiator, taking aim at the Secure Access Service Edge category that several rivals had staked out:

> "We have gone far beyond SASE by pioneering our zero trust exchange. Simply put, we offer better security at lower cost."
>
> — Jay Chaudhry, Q2 FY2025 earnings call, [March 5 2025](https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2025/03/05/zscaler-zs-q2-2025-earnings-call-transcript/)

## The $5 Billion Mandate and the Platform's Third Act

The ambition behind the platform expansion was formalised in September 2024 when Zscaler appointed Adam Geller, a security product veteran, as Chief Product Officer, in a hire explicitly positioned around scaling the business to $5 billion in ARR and beyond. Chaudhry framed Geller's task as building an AI-driven security operations platform — a second architectural layer atop the Zero Trust Exchange. In the same period, the company appointed Phil Tee, a co-founder of enterprise AI monitoring businesses, as Executive Vice President of AI Innovations, and acquired SPLX, a prompt-injection and AI security technology business, to seed the AI Guard product line.

By the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025, the shape of that third act was visible in operating metrics. Revenue grew 21 percent to $719.2 million, ARR crossed $3.015 billion — up 22 percent — and the company posted its highest quarterly operating margin on record, exceeding 22 percent. Chaudhry's characterisation of the demand environment reflected the degree to which AI exposure had become the defining customer anxiety:

> "Zscaler's Zero Trust and AI security solutions are imperative in today's world and are driving robust demand. We recently delivered AI Guardrails for Public and Private apps, and we are rapidly expanding our AI security portfolio to address the emerging risks of AI models and applications."
>
> — Jay Chaudhry, Q4 FY2025 earnings release, [SEC 8-K, July 31 2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368325000138/zs-07312025_991.htm)

Across four fiscal years, Zscaler had scaled from a cloud-native proxy business chiefly selling ZIA and ZPA to an integrated platform whose emerging product lines — AI security, data protection, digital experience monitoring — were by management's account growing at twice the rate of the core. Full-year non-GAAP net income reached $534.8 million against a GAAP net loss that had narrowed to $41.5 million, suggesting the operating leverage inherent in a subscription SaaS model was finally expressing itself at scale. The transition from growth-at-all-costs to growth-with-demonstrated-economics, which Chaudhry had begun signalling with the Rule of 80 commitment in fiscal 2022, had completed its first cycle — and a second, AI-inflected cycle was already underway.

chapters.title: Jay Chaudhry, CFO, executive team, and the board
chapters.body:
## The Founder: From Himachal Pradesh to Silicon Valley

Jay Chaudhry's biography reads, in his own telling, as a parable about the inadequacy of perimeter security long before he coined the phrase. He was born on 26 August 1958 in Panoh, a village of roughly eight hundred people in what is now Himachal Pradesh. Electricity and running water did not reach Panoh until he was a teenager; he walked nearly four kilometres each morning to attend school in the neighbouring village. From that starting point, he earned a Bachelor of Technology in Electronics Engineering from IIT BHU Varanasi, then immigrated to the United States at age twenty-two, completing master's degrees in industrial engineering, computer engineering, and marketing at the University of Cincinnati before later attending Harvard Business School's executive management programme. The arc — from a village without a grid to the boardrooms of IBM, Unisys, and NCR, and then to founding five security companies — gives Chaudhry a biographical claim that few enterprise-software CEOs can match: a visceral understanding of what it means to operate without infrastructure that others take for granted. At sixty-seven, he remained Zscaler's Chairman and Chief Executive Officer as of the frozen snapshot date, having held both titles without interruption since the company's founding in 2007.

## Serial Founder: Four Exits Before Zscaler

Chaudhry built and sold four security companies before Zscaler — SecureIT (VeriSign, 1998), CipherTrust (Secure Computing, 2006 for $274M), CoreHarbor (USi/AT&T), and AirDefense (Motorola, 2008). The pattern across all four: identify an emerging threat vector, build a product, sell to an incumbent. What it never produced was security designed for the cloud from the outset — the gap Zscaler was conceived to fill.

## The 2007 Founding Thesis and the 2018 IPO

The March 2018 IPO validated the architecture thesis. By fiscal year 2025, Chaudhry marked the ARR milestone:

> "We had an outstanding Q4, in which we achieved a new milestone of more than $3 billion of Annual Recurring Revenue while achieving our highest ever operating margin for a quarter.""

## The CFO Transition: Canessa to Rubin

For much of Zscaler's public life, Remo Canessa served as Chief Financial Officer, steering the company through the IPO and the hypergrowth years of fiscal 2019–2023. In 2024 Canessa announced his intention to retire; he remained with Zscaler in an advisory capacity through the end of fiscal year 2025 (31 July 2025) to support the handover. His successor, **Kevin Rubin**, joined Zscaler as CFO on 26 May 2025. Rubin, then fifty-one, brought a specific profile: more than two decades at high-growth public and private technology companies, including eight years as CFO of Alteryx (April 2016–March 2024), during which he also served as interim CEO from January to March 2024, and a subsequent year as CFO of BetterUp. His compensation on appointment was set at a $470,000 annual base salary and a $470,000 target annual bonus under the Employee Incentive Plan, with additional equity grants approved by the Compensation Committee. The hire landed at a pivotal moment — Zscaler was in the first full year of its transition from pure billings-growth narrative to a combined revenue-growth-plus-margin story, and Rubin's public-company operating experience at Alteryx, itself a business that navigated a significant go-to-market reconfiguration, was directly relevant.

## Operating Leadership

Below the CEO and CFO, the operating layer that executed the platform strategy as of the frozen date comprised:

| Executive | Title | Notable Prior Context |
|---|---|---|
| Kevin Rubin | Chief Financial Officer | CFO Alteryx 2016–2024; CFO BetterUp 2024–2025 |
| Adam Geller | Chief Product Officer | Internal Zscaler product leader, age 49 |
| Mike Rich | Chief Revenue Officer & President, Global Sales | Age 58; global enterprise sales leadership |
| Raj Judge | EVP, Corporate Strategy & Ventures | Former Wilson Sonsini Senior Partner; joined May 2025 |
| Robert Schlossman | Chief Legal Officer & Secretary | Age 57; Zscaler general counsel |

Raj Judge's appointment in May 2025 was notable in that Zscaler structured his role explicitly to lead growth strategy, business development, and venture investment initiatives — and simultaneously added him to the board as a Class III director. The dual executive-director status made Judge one of two non-independent directors alongside Chaudhry himself.

## The Board

The board that oversaw Zscaler as of the frozen date comprised nine members, seven of them independent under Nasdaq standards. Three classes of directors serve staggered three-year terms, with the January 2026 annual meeting electing Class II directors Andrew Brown, Scott Darling, and David Schneider for terms running to the company's fiscal 2028 annual meeting.

| Director | Independence | Tenure on Board | Principal Credential |
|---|---|---|---|
| Jay Chaudhry | Non-independent | Since founding (2007) | Chairman, CEO, Founder |
| Raj Judge | Non-independent | May 2025 | EVP Corporate Strategy; former Wilson Sonsini |
| Karen Blasing | Independent | January 2017 | Four-time CFO (Guidewire, Nuance, Force10, Salesforce SVP Finance); Audit Committee Chair |
| Charles Giancarlo | Independent | November 2016 | CEO, Pure Storage; former Cisco EVP; former Silver Lake MD |
| Scott Darling | Independent | November 2016 | President, Dell Technologies Capital; former Intel Capital VP/MD |
| Andrew Brown | Independent | 2015 | Longest-tenured independent director |
| David Schneider | Independent | — | President, Global Customer Operations, ServiceNow; former CRO, ServiceNow |
| Eileen Naughton | Independent | September 2021 | Former Chief People Officer, Google; board member, Ares Management |
| James Beer | Independent | May 2024 | Former CFO, Atlassian; board member, Alaska Air Group, DocuSign |

**Karen Blasing** chairs the Audit Committee and brings the deepest financial governance credentials on the board — four CFO tenures including Guidewire Software, where she led the company's January 2012 IPO and two follow-on offerings. Her presence since January 2017 means she has overseen the Zscaler IPO process alongside Canessa from the governance side. **Charles Giancarlo**, the longest-serving independent director, joined in November 2016, just over a year before the S-1 was filed; his background running the product lines that generated roughly 80 percent of Cisco's revenues in the mid-2000s, and his subsequent CEO role at Pure Storage, gave the board direct hyperscaler-era operating experience. **James Beer**, added in May 2024, deepened the bench of financial expertise at a moment when Zscaler's investors were increasingly focused on margin progression and free-cash-flow generation — his Atlassian CFO tenure coincided with that company's own transition from hypergrowth to scaled-profitability narrative. **Eileen Naughton**'s background as Google's Chief People Officer addresses the talent-governance dimension as Zscaler expanded headcount aggressively through its platform-broadening phase.

## Ownership and Control

The 2025 proxy statement filed in November 2025 disclosed that Chaudhry beneficially owned 26,857,608 shares directly, representing approximately 16.8 percent of shares outstanding as of 1 November 2025. Including indirect holdings through family trusts and affiliated entities, his total beneficial ownership has been estimated at approximately 38 percent of the outstanding stock — a concentration that gives the founder substantial practical influence over matters put to a shareholder vote, even absent a formal dual-class share structure. Zscaler's capital structure is single-class common stock, which means Chaudhry's voting power derives from raw economic ownership rather than super-voting shares; nonetheless, at roughly 38 percent held by a founder who is also full-time CEO and chairman, the governance dynamic at Zscaler more closely resembles a founder-controlled company than a widely dispersed institutional-ownership base, even at a $20-billion-plus market capitalisation. The 2025 proxy noted the board's awareness of the concentration and the Compensation Committee's effort to align long-term equity vesting schedules across the executive team with multi-year performance objectives rather than pure time-based vesting — a structural acknowledgement that succession and ownership-dilution management are active governance questions as the platform matures.

chapters.title: Enterprise, federal, partner channel, go-to-market motion
chapters.body:
## Enterprise Customer Architecture

Zscaler built its commercial engine around a deliberately concentrated targeting strategy: sell the Global 2000 — the world's two thousand largest corporations by revenue — on replacing their network-security perimeter not with better hardware, but with none at all. By the time the company reported fiscal 2024 results in September 2024, that proposition had translated into roughly 8,700 customers and annual revenue of $2.167 billion, a customer base whose composition, increasingly skewed toward multimillion-dollar relationships and US federal agencies, reflected a platform that had escaped commodity positioning and lodged itself in enterprise procurement as a strategic asset.

The consequences of Global 2000 targeting are most legible in the large-customer cohort disclosures Zscaler included in its SEC filings. In fiscal 2022, approximately 340 customers generated more than $1 million in annual recurring revenue, against a total base of roughly 6,700. By fiscal 2024, those figures had grown to approximately 560 customers above the $1 million threshold and more than 34 customers above $5 million, while the total customer count reached approximately 8,700. The widening gap — total customers growing roughly 15% annually while million-dollar customers expanded faster — reflected both the platform's success in winning larger initial deployments and the land-and-expand dynamic as customers layered data-protection and AI-security modules atop the ZIA and ZPA core.

[Zscaler 10-K, fiscal year ended July 31 2024, filed September 2024 via SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=ZS&type=10-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=10)

The named-account model that underpinned this concentrated customer base required a corresponding sales architecture. Enterprise account executives were assigned defined Global 2000 territories and paired with solution architects; a post-sale customer-success function tracked workload deployment depth and module adoption. New logo acquisition was prized, but the subscription economics meant that expansion within the installed base was the dominant revenue-growth lever in any given quarter.

## The Federal Beachhead

President Biden's May 2021 cybersecurity executive order mandated federal zero-trust migration. Zscaler's FedRAMP High authorization — the most demanding compliance tier — positioned it ahead of competitors. DISA became a visible reference customer; multiple civilian agencies followed.

The FY2025 period introduced uncertainty: the second Trump administration's Department of Government Efficiency initiative compressed procurement timelines. Management argued agency zero-trust mandates remained structural compliance obligations, supported by DoD's own zero-trust framework.

## Partner Channel Architecture

Zscaler's relationship with the global systems-integrator community evolved from limited early engagement into a structured co-selling and co-delivery apparatus. By fiscal 2023 and 2024, the most significant SI relationships — Accenture, Deloitte, IBM, Wipro, Infosys, Capgemini, and Tata Consultancy Services among them — were generating partner-influenced pipeline across both new-logo and expansion transactions. These firms trained dedicated Zscaler practices, embedded certified Zero Trust Exchange architects within client engagement teams, and increasingly positioned Zscaler deployments as the security layer inside broader cloud-migration and digital-transformation mandates.

The strategic significance of SI influence was structural. A Global 2000 corporation launching a multi-year cloud infrastructure transformation typically selected a primary systems integrator before selecting individual security vendors; the SI's architectural recommendation could pre-qualify Zscaler or, conversely, entrench a competitor. Zscaler's investment in the partner ecosystem — certification programs, co-marketing funding, joint go-to-market commitments, and dedicated partner-success managers — was as much defensive as it was a new-logo acquisition play.

Managed security service providers formed a distinct channel layer. MSSPs resold and operated the Zero Trust Exchange on behalf of mid-market and enterprise customers lacking internal security-operations resources, extending Zscaler's commercial reach below its direct enterprise sales ceiling. Technology alliances deepened the platform's competitive moat: a joint Zscaler–CrowdStrike deployment correlated zero-trust network telemetry with endpoint-detection data, while integrations with Okta anchored identity-aware access policies to the Zero Trust Exchange enforcement layer. ServiceNow integrations connected Zscaler's risk signals to enterprise IT service-management workflows, making the platform stickier inside large accounts where ServiceNow was already embedded.

Value-added resellers — CDW, Presidio, Insight, and similar North American distributors — handled transactional volume and mid-market coverage, freeing the direct enterprise team to focus on named Global 2000 accounts and large-deal origination.

## Net Retention and the Land-and-Expand Engine

Zscaler's subscription model concentrated financial-performance risk in a single underlying metric: net revenue retention — the proportion of prior-year ARR that renewed and expanded in the current period. The company had historically reported NRR in excess of 120%, indicating that expansions and upsells materially outweighed churn. In later fiscal periods Zscaler shifted public disclosure toward cohort-based large-customer metrics rather than a single consolidated NRR figure, but the operative dynamic remained unchanged: customers initiated deployment with ZIA or ZPA, proved out the architecture in a defined pilot population, and then progressively expanded to ZDX performance monitoring, data-loss prevention, cloud-access security broker functionality, and emerging AI-security and IoT/OT modules.

The pillar-expansion model was integral to the financial pitch to CFOs. An enterprise that had already amortized Zscaler's client-connector deployment and invested in policy migration could add a data-protection pillar at incremental cost and disruption; the marginal economics of adding a SaaS module onto existing infrastructure justified Zscaler's premium relative to point-solution competitors. By fiscal 2024, Zscaler disclosed that a growing share of its customer base consumed three or more product pillars — a metric management cited as evidence of platform stickiness over and above basic renewal rates.

| Customer Cohort Metric | FY2022 | FY2023 | FY2024 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total customers | ~6,700 | ~7,700 | ~8,700 |
| Customers >$1M ARR | ~340 | ~430 | ~560 |
| Customers >$5M ARR | — | — | >34 |
| Revenue (USD) | $1.091B | $1.617B | $2.167B |

*Source: Zscaler 10-K filings, SEC EDGAR*

## Go-to-Market Evolution Into the AI Era

As the fiscal 2025 period opened, Zscaler's go-to-market motion began adapting to a selling environment reshaped by enterprise AI adoption. The proliferation of large-language-model workloads within Global 2000 accounts created demand for security controls specific to AI: protection against data leakage through SaaS-based AI applications, governance over which third-party AI services employees could access, and inspection of API traffic flowing between internal systems and external model endpoints. Zscaler's AI security suite — positioned atop the existing Zero Trust Exchange inline-inspection infrastructure — was marketed as the natural extension of an already-deployed platform, a framing designed to convert the installed base rather than open new competitive evaluations from scratch.

Jay Chaudhry framed the AI moment as a demand accelerant on fiscal 2025 earnings calls, arguing that enterprise AI adoption created fresh urgency around inline traffic inspection and data governance — precisely the capabilities the Zero Trust Exchange had been built to deliver at scale.

The go-to-market motion that had carried Zscaler from founding to $2 billion in revenue — direct enterprise selling into the Global 2000, backed by SI partnerships and an expanding land-and-expand installed base — entered the AI era carrying the structural advantages of incumbency: enforcement infrastructure already deployed across customer networks, trust relationships established through years of subscription renewals, and a cloud-native inline architecture uniquely positioned to inspect the AI-era traffic patterns its enterprise customers were only beginning to generate at volume.

chapters.title: Where Zscaler sits against Palo Alto Prisma, Netskope, Cisco, Cloudflare
chapters.body:
By the time Zscaler's annual recurring revenue crossed $3 billion in mid-fiscal 2025, the company had spent nearly two decades arguing a single architectural proposition: that security should live in the cloud, inline between users and applications, rather than in hardware stacked in corporate data centres. That proposition was, by the spring of 2026, no longer controversial. It had become the organising thesis of the entire enterprise security market — which meant every major vendor in that market was now competing directly with Zscaler.

The competitive field that formed around Zscaler was varied in origin but convergent in ambition. Palo Alto Networks attacked from the established security incumbency, leveraging its dominant firewall franchise and a $6.33 billion Next-Generation Security ARR base to assemble a rival SASE platform. Netskope, a cloud-native proxy pure-play that finally reached public markets in September 2025, contested the same blue-chip enterprise logos with differentiated data-loss prevention. Cisco brought its vast installed networking base and bundling leverage — and the sales reach of 60,000-plus enterprise relationships. Cloudflare arrived from a different direction entirely, building zero-trust access on top of a global content-delivery network that already touched the internet at scale. And behind those four principals, a longer tail of vendors — Forcepoint, Skyhigh Security, Check Point Harmony SASE, Lookout — competed for mid-market share and specialised verticals.

## The Principal Rival: Palo Alto Networks Prisma

No competitive pairing drew more analyst attention through 2025 and into 2026 than Zscaler versus Palo Alto Networks. The two companies had roughly comparable revenues — Zscaler reported $2.673 billion for fiscal year 2025 against Palo Alto's full-year guidance of $11.3 billion, though Palo Alto's total included network security, cloud security, and a large on-premises installed base — but in the specific SASE/SSE contest, the numbers converged more closely. Palo Alto's SASE ARR reached $1.5 billion in the fiscal second quarter of 2026, growing approximately 40 per cent year-on-year, against Zscaler's total company ARR of $3.4 billion growing 25 per cent. The two vendors were, in market-analyst parlance, trading at different multiples on different base sizes, but both were compounding faster than the broader security market.

| Vendor | ARR / NGS ARR (most recent Q) | YoY Growth | Gartner MQ Position |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zscaler | $3.4B (Q2 FY2026, Jan 2026) | +25% | SSE Leader (1st) |
| Palo Alto SASE only | $1.5B (Q2 FY2026, Jan 2026) | ~+40% | SASE / SSE / SD-WAN Leader |
| Netskope | $754M ARR (Q3 FY2026, Oct 2025) | +34% | SSE Leader / Forrester highest |
| Cloudflare | ~$2.4B total rev. run-rate | +31–34% | SASE Visionary |

Palo Alto's competitive pitch rested on two pillars: breadth and depth. Its Prisma Access platform carried the full Layer 7 inspection capability of a next-generation firewall into the cloud, offering packet-level visibility that Palo Alto's marketing teams positioned as superior to what they called Zscaler's "proxy-overlay" approach. Prisma Browser added a natively integrated enterprise browser — serving more than 1,500 enterprise customers with over nine million licences by early 2026 — a capability Zscaler did not match organically, though the company moved to address the gap through its acquisition of browser-security startup SquareX. Palo Alto was, critically, the only vendor recognised as a Gartner Magic Quadrant leader in all three adjacent categories simultaneously: SASE, SSE, and SD-WAN, a distinction its sales teams weaponised in competitive evaluations. The company's [second-quarter FY2026 investor materials](https://www.investing.com/news/company-news/palo-alto-networks-q2-2026-slides-ngs-arr-jumps-33-stock-falls-5-93CH-4511827) showed 1,100-plus "platformized" customers — accounts that had consolidated four or more Palo Alto product families — as evidence that the consolidation trade was going its way.

## Architecture as the Core Argument

Against Palo Alto's firepower, Zscaler returned again and again to architecture. The company's Zero Trust Exchange, built cloud-natively from its 2007 founding rather than cloudified from hardware, operated across more than 150 points of presence and 160 data centres globally by 2025, processing hundreds of billions of transactions per day in-line between users and destinations. The distinction mattered technically: a proxy-based inline model meant Zscaler could inspect, modify, and enforce policy on every byte of traffic traversing its platform, creating a telemetry reservoir that improved machine-learning models in a self-reinforcing loop. The scale of that reservoir — accumulated over eighteen years of cloud-only operation — was not easily replicated.

Jay Chaudhry framed the architectural bet in terms of the AI transition on Zscaler's first-quarter fiscal 2026 earnings call:

> "The best AI security is built on the foundation of Zero Trust."

And on the company's second-quarter call, as the proliferation of AI agents became the dominant enterprise-security narrative:

> "Enterprises will need 'inline policy enforcement at massive scale' as AI agents proliferate."

Zscaler's position was that Palo Alto's NGFW-in-the-cloud approach, however capable, was a different animal — a security inspection appliance delivered as a service rather than a purpose-built cloud fabric. Customers running Prisma Access still typically paired it with a third-party SD-WAN vendor, or with Palo Alto's own Prisma SD-WAN, adding integration complexity. Zscaler, by contrast, had always required no WAN hardware at the edge, and its [Zero Trust Branch](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-first-quarter-fiscal-2026-financial-results) segmentation product — introduced to isolate branch networks without traditional firewalls — extended that no-hardware premise further into campus and industrial environments.

## Netskope: The Pure-Play Challenger

Netskope occupied a narrower but genuine threat. The San Jose-based vendor filed for its initial public offering in August 2025, disclosing $707 million in ARR, growing 33 per cent year-on-year, and completed the offering in September at $19 per share, raising approximately $908 million. By the third fiscal quarter of 2026, ARR had reached $754 million, and the company reported a dollar-based net retention rate of 118 per cent against a base of roughly 4,300 customers, more than 100 of whom paid in excess of $1 million annually.

Netskope's differentiation centred on data security. Its inline Data Loss Prevention and Cloud Access Security Broker capabilities were consistently rated superior to Zscaler's by enterprise security teams in proof-of-concept evaluations, particularly in regulated industries where granular data classification mattered. Forrester's 2025 SASE Wave awarded Netskope the highest composite score among all vendors, ahead of Palo Alto and Zscaler, a recognition that carried weight in accounts where DLP was the primary buying criterion. The company had not, however, resolved its profitability challenge: full-year net losses reached $354.5 million in fiscal 2025, up from $344.9 million the prior year, a trajectory that post-IPO public-market investors would scrutinise closely. Zscaler, by contrast, had been generating positive non-GAAP operating income since fiscal 2020.

## Cisco: The Incumbent Bundler

Cisco's competitive relevance rested less on architectural innovation than on distribution leverage. The company's Cisco+ Secure Connect Now combined Meraki SD-WAN with Umbrella's Secure Service Edge capabilities into a single-vendor SASE offer — directly targeting the large installed base of enterprises already running Meraki campus switches and Catalyst SD-WAN across their branch networks. With more than 60,000 enterprise relationships worldwide and a global sales organisation that dwarfed any pure-play security vendor's, Cisco could attach security subscriptions to hardware refresh cycles in ways Zscaler, Netskope, or Cloudflare could not.

The financial picture, however, was complicated. Cisco's security segment grew 59 per cent in fiscal 2025, a figure inflated by the March 2024 acquisition of Splunk; stripped of that contribution, the underlying security business faced more modest growth, and by Q1 fiscal 2026 the security segment had turned negative year-on-year, declining 2 per cent. Enterprise buyers increasingly distinguished between Cisco's networking-rooted security stack — perceived as stitched-together from Umbrella, Duo, and Meraki acquisitions — and the architecturally coherent platforms of Zscaler or even Palo Alto. [Dell'Oro Group research](https://www.channelfutures.com/sdn-sd-wan/zscaler-palo-alto-networks-cisco-sase-market) identified Palo Alto, Cisco, and Zscaler as the top three vendors in SASE by revenue, but the gap between Cisco's legacy revenue and its cloud-native SASE bookings reflected a transition that remained incomplete.

## Cloudflare and the Network-Centric Insurgents

Cloudflare represented a qualitatively different threat: a vendor approaching zero-trust from the network infrastructure layer rather than from security inspection. Its Cloudflare One platform — combining ZTNA, SWG, CASB, and remote browser isolation — ran on the same global network that already handled a meaningful fraction of the internet's DNS and CDN traffic, giving it inherent performance advantages in latency-sensitive geographies. The company [reported](https://www.investing.com/news/company-news/cloudflare-q1-2026-slides-34-revenue-growth-large-customer-base-surges-93CH-4671018) 34 per cent revenue growth in Q1 2026 and signed what management described as the company's longest SASE contract during the first quarter of 2025. Gartner's 2025 SASE Magic Quadrant classified Cloudflare as a Visionary rather than a Leader — reflecting a platform that was still maturing in enterprise DLP and advanced threat-prevention depth — but the trajectory was upward. BTIG's late-2025 decision to downgrade Zscaler to Neutral, citing "intensifying zero-trust competition," specifically named Cloudflare alongside Netskope as the sources of incremental competitive pressure in the small-to-mid enterprise segment.

## The Longer Tail

Beyond the four principals, a second tier of vendors competed for specific verticals and mid-market accounts. Check Point's Harmony SASE — rebranded and extended to include an enterprise browser in 2025 — earned a strong threat-prevention score in Miercom's 2025 benchmark and appealed to enterprises already standardised on Check Point's firewall estate. Forcepoint and Skyhigh Security (formerly McAfee Enterprise's cloud business, operating under Musarubra/Skyhigh's private-equity ownership) maintained loyal installed bases in data-centric verticals, particularly US federal government and financial services, where policy compliance requirements made their specialised DLP heritage compelling. Lookout served the mobile-centric SSE segment.

None of these vendors individually posed a systemic threat to Zscaler's enterprise motion, but collectively they ensured that competitive intensity across the full market remained high, compression on average selling prices remained a structural reality, and the number of evaluation criteria against which Zscaler had to defend continued to expand.

## The Structural Moat

Zscaler's most durable competitive asset was not any single product but the architecture itself — and the eighteen years of operational data that had accumulated inside it. Every transaction inspected, every policy enforced, every threat blocked added signal to the Zero Trust Exchange's machine-learning models. By early 2026 the company processed hundreds of billions of daily transactions across its global fabric; Chaudhry cited the company as well positioned to surpass $10 billion in ARR over the longer term, implying a belief that the Exchange's data-gravity advantage would compound faster than rivals could replicate it through platform assembly.

That thesis was coherent, though not without stress points. Palo Alto's NGS ARR trajectory — targeting $20 billion by 2030 on the back of its platformization strategy — and Netskope's DLP depth represented genuine architectural challenges to specific Zscaler customer segments. The market itself was growing fast enough — the SSE segment alone was projected by Grand View Research to expand at a 21.9 per cent compound annual rate from $6.26 billion in 2024 to $36.87 billion by 2033 — that multiple vendors could compound simultaneously without fighting purely zero-sum battles. But the platform consolidation pressure that had shrunk the long tail of point-product security vendors in the early 2020s was now pressing on the SASE layer itself. By May 2026, the question for Zscaler was not whether its architecture was sound, but whether it could expand broadly enough — into data security, AI operations, IoT segmentation, and managed detection — to remain the centre of gravity around which customers consolidated, rather than one pillar among many inside a larger Palo Alto or Cisco bundle.
